steps.start_work: Takes the next ready item when a slot is free and has the session manager set up where the work runs and the engineer's session. An item worked on here before takes over its latest earlier work's branch, its worktree (reused when it is there, made afresh from the branch otherwise) and its PR; an item imported with a branch takes that branch and the PR imported with it; any other item gets a new branch from main.
steps.run_tools: Runs the tools the calling cell asked for, from the commits the session manager bundled. When the work comes back from the architect, it runs again only the tools that failed. A tool that fails is retried twice before it counts as failed.
steps.full_ci_on_draft: Catches the draft PR up with main and runs the full CI the project's configuration names on it, running a red check once more on the same commit; checks in the table of known red checks do not count.
steps.choose_checks: Decides what runs next, from whether the design chose adversarial testing, whether the review accepted none, the change reviewed last, each side's last results, and the rows the fix cell answered.
steps.check_plan: Measures on the commit to merge what the PR touches and how much more of each budget it uses, and compares that with the plan segment the work hangs on. With no plan segment there is nothing to break, and the work fits.
steps.merge: Puts the PR in this repository's merge queue; at its turn, catches it up with main, runs the full CI and merges it. On a conflict or a red check, the PR leaves the queue; after its fix it joins the queue again at the end.
steps.watch_main: Watches main and the deployment after the merge. When main turns red it stops this repository's merge queue until the cause is clear, then checks three things mechanically: running again on the same commit, the table of known red checks, and the same check on main's commit before the merge.
steps.ask_architect: Queues what is asked for the architect, waking the architect if it sleeps; the work stops and waits without holding a slot. The architect answers with a reply, brought back unchanged.
steps.ask_owner: Puts what is asked before the owner, as an ask of the owner in the owner's interface, and notifies the owner; the work stops and waits without holding a slot. The owner's chosen option or sentence goes back unchanged to the side that asked.
steps.end_work: Ends the work: ends its sessions and records the end. A work whose whole item went to sub-items ends here without merging, and its item is done once the sub-items are merged. A work that delivered a report and handed in what to do next queues it for the architect as a matter of its own: the latest it handed in, as written, with the report's paths under research/ and the commit the work merged.
steps.wake: Wakes the architect: a wake is a work of the architect's graph, which belongs to no item. It goes on in the session the last wake left; the first wake, and the first after a new policy took effect, start a new one. A wake holds no slot, and only one runs at a time.
steps.submit_changes: Puts every change the wake collected to the owner in one ask, each with its reason, the matter it belongs to and who waits; the owner approves all, some (naming which), or none (saying why). With none collected it puts nothing. The wake does not wait for the answer: once the owner answers, the answer is queued for the architect as a matter of its own, and wakes it.
steps.end_wake: Ends the wake. The architect is woken again by the next matter that comes to its queue, or at the next look it set.
steps.count_trials: Counts how many new sessions in a row read this version of the policy's text and were judged to understand it: two pass it, one asks for another.

actions.lock_acceptance: Writes the design's acceptance conditions onto the item and locks them; if they are the same as those already locked, nothing changes.
actions.lock_new_acceptance: Writes the advisor's new acceptance conditions onto the item and locks them.
actions.post_design_card: When the design tree changed, puts the design card in the database for the owner to rule on, and queues it for the architect to look at: it blocks nothing yet, so the owner can look and stop it early. A card that a new design brings after a redesign replaces the cards of this work the redesign set aside, and keeps what the design said changed from them.
actions.update_design_card: Replaces the work's design card with the one handed in, and keeps what the return says changed from it. Only the decisions that changed go through again; when a decision the owner confirmed changes, the engine tells the owner at once that it must be confirmed again.
actions.replace_design_card: Marks the work's open and ruled design cards as replaced: the owner can no longer rule on them. A new design brings a new design card; without one there is nothing to mark.
actions.notify_pending_approvers: Tells the owner that the design card, not yet confirmed, is holding up the merge.
actions.revert_merge: Opens a PR that reverts the merge and puts it first in this repository's merge queue, so that main recovers within minutes.
actions.reopen_with_fix: Opens a new PR under the same item with the original change plus the fix; the original change is reviewed only where the fix touches it.
actions.report_missing_check: Tells the architect that the full CI in the project's configuration missed the check that broke main, so that it is added.
actions.record_waits: Records the items the architect's reply has this work wait for. The engineer's session is kept, and the work holds no slot while it waits.
actions.record_place: Records where the work runs, and the PR it keeps: every later round runs there, and each push is checked against the last pushed head.
actions.record_tool_runs: Records each run, the pushed head and the PR number under the calling cell.
actions.set_aside_checks: Leaves the checks just chosen unrun: the work takes the interjection to choose the way on, and if that carries on, comes back here and the engine chooses again.
actions.hand_over_to_sub_items: Closes the work's draft PR, if any, saying which sub-items took over the work. The work does not merge; it waits for its sub-items.
actions.wake_architect: Queues each side report for the architect once, due at once, which wakes the architect when no wake runs; one marked urgent that comes while a wake runs is also given to that wake at the top of its next round.
actions.deliver_answers: Sends each answer back to the side that interjected, and records it on the work: those of the answers form, and those a redirect carries.
actions.tell_owner: Puts each message the return tells the owner in the owner's interface, unread, and notifies the owner; the work goes on, and no answer comes back.
actions.open_asks: Puts each choice the architect handed in as open to the owner, as an ask that holds no wake; once the owner answers, the answer is queued for the architect as a matter of its own.
actions.queue_fixes: Queues each place the fifth question found to change as a matter of the kind running_unfit.
actions.hold_for_tidying: Starts no new work while the architect sets the whole straight; the works running go on.
actions.release_tidy_hold: New works start again, if they were stopped to set the whole straight.
actions.hold_for_policy: Holds the architect's side while the policy is set: the matters queued wait, and no new work starts; engineers that ask the architect wait.
actions.release_policy_hold: Lets the architect's side go on: the matters queued are handled again, and new works start.
actions.hold_changes: Holds the matter picked with the changes the architect collected for it: the engineer waiting on it goes on waiting, holding no slot, until the owner approves and the architect replies.
actions.close_matter: Marks the matter picked from the queue as handled by this wake, unless an ask of the owner or changes waiting for approval hold it.
actions.new_architect_session: Ends the architect's session: the next wake starts a new one with the new policy, which answers the first question from the start.
actions.queue_policy_changed: Queues a matter of the kind policy_changed at the head of the architect's queue, ahead of those already waiting.

checks.research_only: The worktree is clean, and the commits new in this round touch only `research/`.
checks.design_paths_unchanged: Nothing in the design paths changed in this round: the engine compares them on the branch at the start of the round and at its return. The design tree changes only when designing, implementing and fixing.
checks.measure_matches_runs: An answer of measured has this work's measure runs in this cell among the engine's records; an answer of not_measured has none.
checks.design_card_matches_tree: The design paths changed on the branch and are committed. Each decision on the design card matches a changed node (except those it says sub-items carry, which are not on this branch), and every changed node is on the design card. A decision it says comes from the parent is word for word that section of the parent's design card. An answer of unchanged changed nothing; a report can only answer unchanged; an answer of design_paths_only changed nothing outside the design paths.
checks.design_tree_check: When the design paths changed, the design tree check the project's configuration names passes on the branch, given the fork point with main.
checks.acceptance_matches_locked: Locked acceptance conditions are handed in word for word; to change them, the agent asks the advisor with the kind acceptance_change first. Those the advisor changed, or the owner changed in a ruling on the design card, were locked by the engine then. A work that delivers a change has no report_answer condition.
checks.chosen_matches_ruling: When the owner chose another approach for a decision in a ruling on the design card, the new design card's decision in the same node chooses it; otherwise the agent asks the owner first.
checks.head_pushed_and_green: The head is the local HEAD, the worktree is clean, it was pushed with ci, and the latest fast CI run on it is green.
checks.branch_changes_fit_work: Against main, an implementation change has some change, otherwise the agent asks (another PR may have fixed it); a change to the design paths only changes nothing outside them; a report changes nothing outside `research/`.
checks.conditions_cover_acceptance: There is a row for each acceptance condition (at a re-check, each row names an existing condition); the tests named are on the branch, and the report sections named are in the report.
checks.new_test_results: When the design chose no adversarial testing: each new-behaviour test's two results match the ci and ci_before runs the engine recorded; one red after the change or green before it is fixed in this round.
checks.guard_test_results: When the design chose no adversarial testing: each old-behaviour test's two results match the ci and ci_before runs the engine recorded; one red in either run, or unable to run before the change, is fixed in this round. Each new test is in the table its kind in the test changes says.
checks.adversarial_test_results: Each row's two results match the ci and ci_before runs the engine recorded; at a re-check, those red or disputed last time were run again; when tests were written, the head was pushed with ci.
checks.test_kinds_match: Tests the engineer added are in the table of the kind the engineer gave in the test changes. A test the adversarial tester wrote whose result before the change does not fit its kind is fixed in this round and run again.
checks.design_card_when_tree_changed: The engine compares the design paths on the branch with the version the last design card matched: if they changed and this round handed in no new design card, or did not change and it handed one in, the return is rejected.
checks.tests_only: The commits from the head the engineer handed over to this head touch only the test paths the project's configuration names.
checks.disputed_tests_answered: At a re-check, there is a row for each test the engineer called test_wrong or answered advisor_ruled.
checks.no_insisting_after_ruling: What the engineer answered advisor_ruled is not insisted on, nor marked not_fixed.
checks.fact_basis_ran: A basis of fact names a run the engine recorded, and its result is what that run gave.
checks.conclusions_cover_questions: A report hands in a conclusion for each report_answer condition; other work hands in none.
checks.columns_answered: There is exactly one row for each column the engine listed in this round; with no column listed, none is handed in.
checks.evidence_holds: The evidence is there; the files and lines cited are in the diff; the nodes listed exist; for a changed node, its ancestors were read too.
checks.previous_findings_answered: At a re-review, there is a row for each finding of last time.
checks.no_adversarial_when_due: At the first review of a change whose design chose no adversarial testing and ran none late, no_adversarial is handed in; at a re-review, only does_not_stand; otherwise none.
checks.blind_findings_carried: After a blind review, each of its findings is either among some column's findings with the same number, or withdrawn; every number withdrawn is one the blind review handed in.
checks.table_answered: Every row of the table is answered once, with an answer the table allows for that row.
checks.no_disagreeing_after_insist: A finding the review insisted on, or a test adversarial testing insisted on, is not answered disagree or test_wrong again; when neither side gives way, the engineer asks.
checks.not_caused_by_change: For a red check said not to be caused by the change, the engine checks it itself: a flaky one was run again, and one red on main was seen red there.
checks.ruling_matches_advisor: This work did ask the advisor about this row, and the ruling written matches the advisor's reply.
checks.owner_kinds_to_owner: A point of a kind in the owner_only group is asked of the owner.
checks.answers_match_speakers: Each answer goes to a side that interjected in this round, one answer per side.
checks.design_card_disagreement_redirects: When this round's interjections hold a disagreement with a decision of the design card, the return is a redirect, not answers.
checks.design_card_changed_when_replacing: A design card handed in when this work has handed in one before says what changed from it and why; the work's first design card says nothing of the kind.
checks.constitution_covered: There is exactly one row for each article of each project's constitution the architect is given, in the constitution's order.
checks.chosen_first: The matter chosen is the first of the ranked list; one given by its number in the queue is in the queue and not handled.
checks.changes_valid: Every change has its reason; an item created has its project, title, problem, why, acceptance, level, deliverable, what it touches and where it goes, and a key no other change uses; a split gives each acceptance condition of the item split to one new item at most, one of its locked conditions when its acceptance is locked; what the rules fix holds: after the dependencies and moves, the items' dependencies and the segments' order have no cycle, every item reaches a segment through the items that depend on it, an item touches only what its segment may touch, each budget's shares add up to no more than its line, and a segment removed has no unfinished item. Otherwise the return is sent back.
checks.question_answered: For an engineer's question: with no change waiting for approval, this round replied to it with reply; with changes waiting for approval, it did not reply yet.
checks.approved_written: For the owner's approval: every change approved was written with db_write, and every engineer waiting for them was replied to.
checks.policy_text_clean: The policy quotes none of the owner's words, and holds none of the probes; it names no cell of the flow and no date the owner said something.
checks.probes_cover_points: Every probe names points the text has, and every point has at least one probe.
checks.failed_probes_gone: No probe a new architect answered wrongly is among the probes.
checks.reading_complete: Every point of the policy is restated, and every probe is answered.

inputs.free_slots: The free slots, and the machines with room, as each machine's session manager reports.
inputs.project_guide: The project's AGENTS.md, and the index of the design tree (a title and one sentence per node), with the full text of the nodes the item cites.
inputs.local_commits: The bundle of the work's local commits the session manager made (git bundle).

rules.name: general
rules.desc: How every agent works, whatever its cell
text: Check each fact when you write it: resolve with a tool every commit id, path, number and measurement you report as fact. Another agent's or a reviewer's report is only a lead.
Keep nothing in the command line's own memory: what must last goes into this round's return.

Describe work in plain engineering wording, as in ordinary technical documentation: what was done and why. No adversarial metaphors or phrasing; a model's safety check may misread them and stop the work.
When your own permission check refuses an action, do not have another agent do it, and do not reach it by another route: ask the owner to allow it.

Builds, tests, checks and measurements run in CI, through the tools ci and measure. Never run heavy work on this machine (compiling, type checking, building, test suites, benchmarks, measurements), even when it looks quicker; commands that finish in seconds without loading the processors are fine. sqlite3 runs only as `sqlite3 -safe -readonly <database> ...`, and python3 does not run at all.
Stop only processes you started, by the process id you kept when you started them; never by name or pattern: other sessions and the system's own services run the same commands.

Do not wait within a round: no sleep, no polling, no watching a run, nothing left in the background waiting for something outside. What must be waited for goes to the engine in your return, as tools or an ask.

Subagents only do chores within this round, such as reading documents or searching code: at most `agents.subagents.most` of them, each on a model no larger than your own. They never stand in for an engineer, a reviewer or another cell's agent.

Read only what the question needs: find the place first (grep, `git diff --stat`), then read that range, not the whole file or diff. Do not reread what this session already read, unless it changed or the session was compacted since.

flows.name: engineer

lines.name: engineer
lines.desc: The engineer doing this work: cell 1 starts a new session, and research, design, implementation, fixes and choosing the way on all continue it

lines.name: review
lines.desc: The reviewer: the first review starts a new session, and the blind review, the table review, the design tree review and re-reviews all continue it

lines.name: adversarial
lines.desc: The adversarial tester: the first time starts a new session, and re-checks continue it

lines.name: advisor
lines.desc: The advisor for this work alone: the first question starts a new session, and every later question continues it

rules: Before each round the engine looks at how large the line's session has grown; at the limit, it starts a new session on the same line, which holds nothing yet, so it is given everything this cell's round needs. The worktree stays; the agent rereads the code it needs. The limit is set below the point where Claude Code compacts on its own; the number stays open until it has been measured at what size carrying on costs more than starting afresh.

Compaction still happens, for instance when a session fills up within a round. The session's record marks the compaction, and the session manager sees it: right after the compaction, the session manager gives the rules and inputs this cell got in this round again, then has the agent carry on. From then on the engine treats it as a new session and gives later cells what they need as usual.
A cell on no line starts a session of its own every round, and the engine gives it every input.

When an agent hands in pause, the engine runs the same cell again in the same session: it gives the cell's always inputs again, saying to carry on, and refers to what the session already holds instead of giving it again. If the session was replaced or compacted, the two rules above say what is given again.

rules.name: engineering
rules.desc: How an engineer works: writing code, design, evidence, experiments and the repository. The advisor is an engineer too
text: Writing code: before changing anything, read what governs it: the design tree nodes it touches and their ancestors, the project's references, and the documents that define it.
Writing code: implement the general behaviour. No test, example, client or benchmark selects a special path; no fallback hides an unsupported feature.

Writing code: judge correctness against an oracle independent of the code (the project's oracles, the setting `project.oracles`), such as a reference implementation, a specification, a test suite or a format's conformance files; never the code's own earlier output.
Writing code: ported code keeps its license notice beside it.
Writing code: a small defect outside the task in a file you are already changing, fix it and say so in the PR description; any other defect outside the task goes into side reports.

Design and architecture: examine the responsibilities, interfaces, representations and consumers the change touches for design gaps and clearly better designs. A defect outside the scope goes into side reports, or to the advisor as an ask.

Design and architecture: architecture beyond your own item (how modules relate, their interfaces and contracts, the formats components exchange) is not yours to change. If an interface is not enough, show it with a minimal example and ask the owner, with the kind cross_project_interface.

Priorities: after the project's own priorities, first make the implementation understandable and easy to change. Add only the evidence needed to trust the current result. Defer robustness, infrastructure and polish that no current work needs.

Evidence: a passing result is evidence only if a wrong result would have failed it. Prefer an observation that separates two hypotheses. Before trusting a new check, watch it fail once for each condition it protects, in CI too. Read an exit code from the command itself, not through a pipe.

Evidence: a pass reached by weakening a requirement counts for nothing. Every removed, skipped, narrowed, regenerated or weakened test or check has a technical reason in the same change. A tool's limitation, a timeout or an unimplemented feature never changes an expected result. New or changed check machinery shows that a representative wrong result or missing input is detected; reusing established machinery needs no new demonstration.

Evidence: a bug fix gets a case that fails before the fix and passes after. New behaviour gets coverage of normal use and of its relevant failures and boundaries; existing coverage that exercises the change suffices, and a prose-only edit needs no test. A negative case must fail for the intended reason.
Evidence: before any build, test, measurement or experiment whose duration you have not seen, run the smallest useful sample first.
Evidence: say whether each claim is a goal, a proposal, an implemented capability or a measurement on a given day.
Evidence: research records and other old material are evidence only: their commands, process and proposals are not current requirements.

Evidence: every new test says how long it runs alone and why that time is worth it: what it catches that no other test catches, and why it cannot be smaller, faster or folded into another test. The review challenges that from the opposite side. Time spent for nothing is waste however small; time a test needs is worth it however long.

Experiments: for a chosen direction, open an investigation in `research/`. Before measuring, write the question, the comparison that could answer it either way, and the result that would reject the proposal; a prediction without that prior criterion is exploratory. Report a conclusion no wider than what was tested.

Experiments: before a measurement expected to run 20 minutes or more, write every side to compare (including the sides that would locate the cause of a change, if one shows) and what each result would show; then measure them all in one run. Start a follow-up measurement only when the first one's result raises a question you could not have foreseen, and say in this round's return why it could not answer it.

Experiments: a performance comparison names the workload, machine, versions and settings, and gives every side the same conditions. Precise timing runs on the machine set aside for it (the setting `machines.timing`), one run at a time.

Experiments: decide whether performance changed from measured noise, never from a picked threshold such as 1% or 5%. Run the same source before (base) and after (candidate) in interleaved pairs, with a twin of the base as a control, whose difference from the base is this run's noise. For each workload class on each machine, record the usual noise once as the floor; a run noisier than the floor does not count. If the 95% interval of the candidate-to-base ratio lies wholly on the slower side, it is a regression of any size; wholly on the faster side, an improvement; across 1, no detected change; if it does not decide, add pairs. To attribute a change to this work, add a check that could refute the attribution. Accepting a detected regression is the owner's, asked with the kind accept_slowdown. Report the pairs, noise, floor, interval and verdict.

Design judgment: judge a design only on itself: correct, elegant, sound, maintainable, robust. How much code, tests and documents it changes, how hard it is to build and what it costs are no reason for or against it; cost decides only which work comes first.
Design judgment: work a design needs only because of a poor abstraction is a flaw of that design.
Design judgment: how often a form appears in a project's own tests and programs is no evidence of how much real programs need it.
The repository: put new material in the directory that owns its kind; when none fits, ask the advisor.

The repository: create a file, directory, script or document only when you can say whom it serves, where it lives and when it will be removed. A script is wired to a caller or deleted after its one use; a document is kept current or deleted. Prefer native tooling; a new script says why the native path cannot do the job.
The repository: when new material replaces old, update, merge or delete the old in the same change. Do not move paths that specifications, tests, scripts and gates pin.

The repository: keep other people's changes in a dirty worktree, and change only what the task covers. Keep scratch output, personal paths, machine addresses, keys, credentials and machine-local settings out of the repository, its commit messages and its PR descriptions: once a repository is public, its whole history is visible. Machine setup belongs in the system's configuration.

The repository: a document holds only what serves its reader, with no editorial history or process mixed in. One place defines a thing; other places point to it. A reference resolves to its target, and a cited passage supports the claim.

rules.name: design_tree_writing
rules.desc: What the design tree records, how it is written and when it changes: whenever design, implementation or a fix changes the design tree, this applies
text: The design tree records the key technical decisions this project rests on: what was chosen, why, and what was not chosen. It is organized by concept, not by the layout of the code: a tree is one root node file `design/<concept>.md` under `design/`, with its child nodes in the directory of the same name, `design/<concept>/`, as deep as needed.

Any change to the design paths the project's configuration names gives a design card. Design paths that are not in the node format (a specification, for instance) are changed as the project's AGENTS.md says.

The tree is written for the agents that will change the code later and kept for the long term; the design card is written for the owner. Derivations, measurements and point-by-point comparisons go in `research/`; a node states only conclusions, and its reasons link straight to the section of the research notes.

Record only key decisions: those that affect later implementation or the overall architecture. A decision is a real choice between several workable approaches, even one that looks obvious: it changes accepted behaviour or persistent state, a condition of safety or trust, a shared interface or representation, a clear performance commitment, or a lasting rule of the project. How big the work is or how many files it changes is no reason; a matter with only one workable approach is not recorded. Hold the granularity: too fine, and decisions drown in detail; too coarse, and important choices go unguarded.

Say which kind of ground a reason is: a derivation states its premises and only the conclusions they give; an observation states what was seen and under what conditions; a principle or a single measurement shows only that the choice is suitable, not that it is the only one. Write the reasons when choosing, not afterwards.

A decision that cannot be settled during design still goes into the tree. A provisional one says in its reasons why it is decided this way for now, what is uncertain and when it would be reopened; one still to check says what assumption the work goes on under and how it will be checked. The design card marks the decision provisional or to check. When it is settled later, the node is changed and a new design card handed in as usual.

The node format (the engine checks it when a round returns, and rejects the return if it fails): one node per file, named after the decision it governs; inside, one or more `Decision:` lines, optionally followed by a `Rejected:` list. Each field takes one line, with a blank line between fields; list items follow straight after the heading or the previous item. The tree uses ASCII only.

`Decision:` states the choice, with the reason after `because`, the approach not chosen after `instead of`, or both; at least one of the two. Each `Rejected:` line reads `- <approach>: rejected because <reason>`, and the reason says how it differs from the chosen one, not just the choice turned around. Write for someone who has not seen the original material: spell out abbreviations and short names.
A node holds no dates, history or progress; measurements and facts appear only as evidence in reasons, and anything mentioned is named for what it is, without dates or numbers.

Before changing the tree, apply three filters: it is a decision, not a description, so a node that only describes is not wanted; it records the grounds, not the code, so an interface or implementation with no alternative to compare does not go in; a shared rule is written once, on the common ancestor. Keep each decision short: the choice, the deciding reason or the approach not chosen, and the qualifications needed to keep the meaning.
To bring back a rejected approach, first say what has changed.

The tree and the implementation change together: during design, change the nodes on the branch, commit them locally and write the design card; when a later round changes the tree again, its return carries the whole design card as it stands after the change. If the code holds an important design choice the tree does not yet have, add it. Before changing a node, read it and its ancestors.

Approaches the design card did not choose that are worth remembering go into the node's `Rejected:`, with the reasons the design card gives. When the owner confirms the change, what the design card chose is the node's decision; when the owner chooses another approach, the work goes back to design and the tree changes with it.

rules.name: design_tree_review
rules.desc: How the review reviews the design tree and the design in the code: it applies to a work that does not change the design tree too
text: Review by the points below: the change to the design tree, the whole change, and the existing nodes concerned with their ancestors. A work that does not change the design tree is reviewed too: does a node govern each design choice in its code?

Design card against tree: each decision on the design card says the same thing as the change to its node on the branch; the approaches the design card did not choose that are worth remembering are in `Rejected:`; a decision marked provisional says in the node's reasons what is uncertain and when it would be reopened; one marked to check says what assumption the work goes on under and how it will be checked.

Is it a decision: each node added or changed meets the node format and the three filters. Report nodes that describe and decide nothing, rejection reasons that go in circles, and choices or grounds that cannot be understood without the original material.

Consistency: compare each changed node with its ancestors and siblings, and widen to related decisions where needed; for a change that governs a whole concept, read its whole subtree. Say which nodes you read; for every conflict, narrowing or broken dependency, quote both sides.

Is the architecture right: for each structural choice, were holes in the design and better designs looked for while making and changing it, and can the owner see what was found? The returns of comparing approaches and of thinking again whether there is a better design are among your inputs. Report a concrete hole, or a clearly better design, left unaddressed; something deferred that is not recorded in the database counts too. Judge by what was built and the grounds recorded for it; do not demand imagined generality, and do not supply reasons for it after the code is written.
In the four points below, "code" means everything that implements a decision, specifications and configuration included; widen to affected users where needed.

Decisions in the code: for each change that embodies a design choice, point to the node that governs it; report one with no node as a missing change to the design tree. Ordinary implementation steps need no node.
Contradiction: report code that contradicts a decision, or implements a rejected approach, without a change to the tree that replaces the decision.
Orphans: for code removed, find decisions left with no implementation; report a retired approach whose rejection reason is not recorded, and a rejected approach still in the implementation.

Incomplete: for each design commitment in scope, find the behaviour and conditions that support it; report what is missing, half done, a placeholder, or short of evidence. A single related function does not make it done. Design unrelated to this work, and anything explicitly deferred, is out of scope, unless the deferral contradicts this work's scope or its claim to be done.
To check: each to-check this work adds is either checked, or says why it stays and which work will check it; report one with neither as a finding.
The numbers the design tree check prints (nodes, depth, decisions, compared with the fork point) are among your inputs; report on them.

rules.name: review_table
rules.desc: Which columns the engine lists for the table review: one table for a work that delivers a change and one for a report, and a further round for a work that changes the design tree
text: The review table is the list the engine puts in the question for the review: one number per column, one row of answer per column. Below is which columns the engine lists. At a re-review it lists only the columns to review this time: when reviewing what changed, the columns the changed part concerns; when looking at disputes only, none.
Every work that delivers a change has these columns:
The change matches the design: it does everything the design and the design card say, and nothing more.

The implementation is correct: its behaviour is general, with no path special to one test, example, customer or measurement, and no fallback that hides an unsupported feature; correctness is judged against an independent reference, not against the code's own earlier output.

The tests catch errors: a wrong result turns a test red; a bug fix has an example that is red before the change and green after; new behaviour is covered for normal use, errors and edge cases; the fast CI reaches the change.
A measured slowdown: always a finding, however small; only the owner can accept a slowdown.

Replies were followed: the replies of the advisor, the architect and the owner on this work, and each way on the engineer chose; a reply that plainly says to change the design, or that what the work must deliver has changed, but the implementation did not follow, is a finding.

Design in the code is governed by nodes: review by the four points on code against decisions in the design tree review (decisions in the code, contradiction, orphans, incomplete); a work that does not change the design tree is reviewed too.

Repository hygiene: anything added at the root was agreed by the owner; a dependency's version that moved says which version and why, and that version is on its repository's main; no local paths, machine addresses or credentials; each new file can say whom it is for and when it will be removed; the documents changed with the code.
The review list in the project's configuration: one column per entry.
A work that delivers a change also has columns made from the work itself:
One column per acceptance condition: can it be checked; is the evidence there, does it come from the head to be merged, and does it hold.

One column per judgment in the research and design: the work stands; there is no better design; and for each check answered "no" (a gap in what is under test, unsure facts, architectural burden, cross-project dependency, splitting), its reason.
One column per workaround and per design change: does its reason hold, and did the design change with it.
One column per test or check removed, skipped or relaxed: compared with before, is there a technical reason; a compiler limitation, a timeout or an unimplemented feature is no reason.

One column per new test: take the other side on its running time. Do other tests already catch what it catches, could it be smaller or faster, could it be folded into another test? If the writer's reasons can be knocked down, it is a finding.

A work that delivers a report has another table: one column per acceptance condition, for which section of the report answers it and whether the answer is right; whether the evidence supports the conclusions; whether the approaches compared ran under the same conditions (the same load, machine, versions and settings); whether a conclusion claims more than was measured; whether it can be reproduced (the measurement code and commands are in the repository and rerun as written); whether "what to do next" holds; and, as for a change, one column per judgment in the research and design.

A work that changes the design tree has, after the table review, a round of its own for the design tree: one column for each point of the design tree review: design card against tree, is it a decision, consistency, is the architecture right, to check, and the numbers the design tree check prints. The four points on code against decisions were reviewed in the table review and are not answered again.

rules: The owner's interface shows two things for each work: its stage, and what it is doing or waiting for right now, such as "running the full CI" or "waiting for the owner to confirm the design card".
The stage is not stored: it follows from the cell the work is at. The engine records that cell anyway, and the table below gives its stage.

While asking someone (the advisor, the architect or the owner), choosing the way on, or running tools, the stage is that of the cell the work stopped at: a question to the advisor during design is still at the design stage.
unready and queued come before this flow starts: once an item is written and queued, it goes from unready to queued. A work can be cancelled at any cell; cancelled is an end too.

list.name: unready
list.desc: The item is still being written: its problem and acceptance are not ready, and work cannot start

list.name: queued
list.desc: The item is written and queued, waiting for a slot; when work starts, the engine gives it a machine and a session here

list.name: research
list.desc: Researching the problem itself, and judging whether the work stands

list.name: design
list.desc: Comparing approaches, choosing one, writing the design, and the checks after design

list.name: implement
list.desc: Changing the code by the design, or doing the research and writing the report

list.name: test_and_review
list.desc: Adversarial testing, the full CI on the draft, review, fixes, and the engine choosing what runs next

list.name: merge
list.desc: Judging whether the work may enter the merge queue; in the queue, catching up with main, running the full CI and merging

list.name: done
list.desc: Main and the deployment are green

list.name: cancelled
list.desc: The owner or the architect cancelled it: a work can be cancelled at any cell, so no row leads here

roles.name: advisor
roles.desc: This work's advisor, one level above you: technical judgment, such as whether the design, the approach or the acceptance must change, and what you are unsure of or cannot decide; when you must judge first to know whether it is for the owner, ask the advisor first too

roles.name: architect
roles.desc: The one architect over everything: what touches other items or the overall structure, such as splitting off sub-items, adding dependencies, duplicating another item, or a root cause in another item or project

roles.name: owner
roles.desc: What only the owner can do or decide: the owner_only group of the ask kinds may be asked of the owner only; what only the owner can fix, such as missing credentials or a permission block, goes to the owner too. Technical judgment goes to the advisor, and what crosses items to the architect

fields.desc: For something the owner must decide, the choice: options, a recommendation, how sure you are; not for something the owner only has to do (a permission, credentials, configuration). Write every text in it in the owner's language (the setting `owner.language`), as `format:common` says a field the owner reads is written, with technical terms in their English original

limits.where: Every loop has a counter, on the row that closes the loop: the engine adds one each time it takes the row, and never resets it during the work. The counters are in this work's database records and visible in the owner's interface. The limits are numbers in the project's configuration, next to the CI settings; a counter with no number is only counted, never reported.
limits.waits: A row that waits for someone (19 waiting for items it depends on to merge, or for the owner to confirm the design card) counts nothing: what it waits for is the owner or another work, and this work is not turning; how long it waited is visible in the owner's interface.
limits.over: Past a limit, the engine still takes the row and tells the owner in the owner's interface, without stopping: for now it only records and reports, it does not block; real problems are looked at one by one.

counters.name: asks
counters.desc: The times the cells asked the advisor, the architect or the owner, each question once whomever it went to, including questions the advisor and the architect asked themselves

counters.name: tool_requests
counters.desc: The times the cells asked the engine to run tools, each return once

counters.name: tool_failures
counters.desc: The times a tool failed, the engine's two retries failed too, and the architect was asked: the tools 13 runs and 7, 9 and 10 all count

counters.name: fixes
counters.desc: The times 8 returned from a fix, whether adversarial testing, the full CI, the review or the merge queue sent it there

counters.name: late_adversarial
counters.desc: The times the review needed no fix but only late adversarial testing

counters.name: main_red
counters.desc: The times main went red or the deployment failed after the merge, and the cause was found to be a changed environment (asking the architect) or this merge (back to 8 to fix)

counters.name: redesigns
counters.desc: The times 2b found a better design and went back to 2 to compare again

counters.name: total_time
counters.desc: The time agents spend working on this work, plus the time of the tools they have the engine run; waiting for the owner, for a slot or for a machine's queue is recorded apart and not counted. The engine looks each time an agent's round returns, so every cell is covered; when a stretch's budget is used up, the engine has the agent pause, and the pause goes back to the agent's own loop, the only one it governs

counters.name: flow_anomalies
counters.desc: The times the engineer, choosing the way on, chose a way that did not fit the situation, and the engine stopped and reported it to the owner

counters.name: interjections
counters.desc: The times an agent returned after an interjection: answers, redirect, and a work at an engine step sent straight to choose the way on all count

counters.name: waits_for_items
counters.desc: The times the architect had this work stop and wait for other items, and the engineer stopped to wait when choosing the way on

kinds: The existing architecture or design has a flaw this work cannot get around
It is harder than the level you were given, and you cannot judge it
The behaviour something the project specifies must have (a language, a format, a protocol) has to be decided
It touches a safety guarantee the project makes
An interface, convention or data format between projects must change

What is under test (named in the project's configuration) rejects a natural way of writing something, or handles it badly. In what, give the code you want to write, the error it really gives (run it, not from memory), and why this way of writing it is natural
A fact not yet checked would change the direction if it were wrong. In what, say what you are unsure of, which fact would change the direction, and how to check it

This work cannot be done in one PR and must be split. In what, say what each sub-item does and what the parent keeps. If it was split before, ask, given the sub-items already split off, whether what remains must be split again

The problem is not worth solving, or the item is framed wrongly: the pain does not exist, solving it would not remove the pain, or the item's scope, deliverable or place is wrong. In what, say where it does not stand and why you judge so
After comparing, no approach can be chosen. In what, say where it is stuck and what is missing to decide
The approach the design chose does not work, or a fact it rests on is wrong, and it must be redesigned. In what, say which one and how you found out
An acceptance condition itself must change. In what, say which one and why
You cannot resolve a merge conflict with main. In what, say where the conflict is and why you cannot resolve it
It duplicates another work, and this work must stop until someone decides
It cannot go on until another item or project delivers something. In what, say which project, what it must deliver, and the items already in the database for it

If the reply or interjection plainly says to change the design, or that what this work must deliver has changed, choose accordingly; a disagreement with the design card cannot carry on. If the reply has this work stop and wait for other items to deliver, choose wait_for_items: the engine stops this work to wait for them and keeps the session; do not carry on first or change the design first, but decide when they have delivered. While still researching, there is no design to change. If the architect split off sub-items, this work's design and estimate still cover the whole, and it must redesign for the part that remains. If everything went to sub-items and this work keeps nothing, there is no way on to choose here: hand in carry_on as next, as anything else is a flow anomaly, and write in progress what the sub-items need to know when they take over, such as how far it got and what is on the branch; the engine ends this work. If you choose a way that cannot be chosen in the situation, the engine does not go on but marks a flow anomaly and hands it to the owner. If you lack one fact to decide, ask again; do not question the reply you brought back. In progress, write what you decided and why.

reply: You asked someone earlier, and the reply is in the input. It answers what you asked, and may also say in passing that the design must change, or that what this work must deliver has changed. If a fact the reply rests on is wrong, ask again, saying which fact.
interjection: In another cell you got an interjection, thought what comes next might change, and handed in redirect to come here. The interjection is in the session: read it again from the start and work out what the speaker wants; when the owner and the architect say different things, the owner's word goes. If on reflection nothing needs to change, choose carry_on and go back to that cell.
interjection_at_engine: While the work stood at one of the engine's own steps (such as choosing what runs next, or waiting to merge), an interjection came for you: it is at the top of the input, and you have not read it yet. Read it and work out what the speaker wants; when the owner and the architect say different things, the owner's word goes. If you choose carry_on, the work goes back to that step and the engine judges again.
waited: The items you stopped to wait for are all merged, and what they delivered is in the input. Work out whether what they delivered is what this work expected: if so, carry on; if not, decide by where it differs whether to change the design or whether what this work must deliver has changed.

out.name: next
out.desc: By the reply brought back, how you go on

cases.name: redesign_in_research
cases.note: A flow anomaly: still researching, there is no design to change. The owner gets the reply or interjection brought back, the way the engineer chose and its progress; when the owner answers, the work comes back here to choose again.

cases.name: carry_on_unfit
cases.note: A flow anomaly: carrying on makes no sense after sub-items were split off (the design and estimate still cover the whole) or with a disagreement with the design card. The owner gets the reply or interjection brought back, the way the engineer chose and its progress; when the owner answers, the work comes back here to choose again.

cases.name: should_wait
cases.note: A flow anomaly: the architect's reply has the work wait for other items, and the engineer did not choose to wait. The owner gets the reply, the way the engineer chose and its progress; when the owner answers, the work comes back here to choose again.

cases.name: nothing_to_wait_for
cases.note: A flow anomaly: the engineer chose to wait with no item to wait for. The owner gets the reply, the way the engineer chose and its progress; when the owner answers, the work comes back here to choose again.

cases.name: all_split_but_changed
cases.note: A flow anomaly: the architect gave all of the work to sub-items, so there is no design to change and nothing to research again. The owner gets the reply, the way the engineer chose and its progress; when the owner answers, the work comes back here to choose again.

stage: The cell the work stopped at was still researching: the problem itself, or whether this work stands
The cell the work stopped at was in design or after it
split: In the reply brought back, the architect split off sub-items, and this work keeps a part
The reply brought back split off no sub-item
In the reply brought back, the architect gave all of this work to sub-items, and it keeps nothing
