In another cell the engineer got an interjection, thought what comes next might change, and handed in redirect
While the work stood at one of the engine's own steps, an interjection came for the engineer, and the engine sent it straight here
The items this work stopped to wait for are all merged, and the engine came back here with what they delivered
must_wait: The architect's reply has this work stop now to wait for other items, and some are not merged yet
No item to wait for now
design_card_disputed: The reply or interjection brought back holds a disagreement with the design card (the owner's)
No disagreement with the design card

nodes.title: Back to the cell that asked

inputs.what: Recorded by the engine: the cell this work asked from (the engine records the step it stopped at, and where it goes on when the reply comes)

nodes.title: Wait for other work to deliver

inputs.what: The items to wait for: those the architect's reply lists, each with what it must deliver and how far it is

cases.name: waited
cases.note: The engine goes back to choose the way on with what they delivered.

cases.name: waiting
cases.note: The owner's interface shows which items the work waits for; the engineer's session is kept, and the work holds no slot.

cases.name: interjection
cases.note: The engine takes the interjection to choose the way on; if that still waits, the work comes back here to wait.

waited: Every item waited for is merged

nodes.title: Advisor

inputs.what: What is asked: from which cell (recorded by the engine), its kind, the question and the reasons
What the cell that asked did in this round

This work's research and design: the engineer's understanding, the approaches compared and the chosen design, as far as the work has come; coming from 1 or 1a there are no approaches compared yet, and when 1 only asked there is no understanding either
The estimate in the design; none before design is done
Where the implementation departed from the plan (the engine accumulates them over the rounds); none unless coming from implementation or a fix
The architect's or the owner's replies; none if they were not asked
How many times this work has asked

prompt: You are the advisor of this work, one level above its engineer, and for this work alone. What you are asked is yours to decide: research it through before deciding, find the root, and judge a design only on itself, not on how much it changes. This work's own item is yours to rule on: if the design must change, or the problem itself must, say so plainly in the reply; the engineer goes back to change the design or research again by it. You may also change the locked acceptance: write the new acceptance conditions in the reply, and the engine puts them on the item and locks them. Items in other trees or other projects are not yours, nor is splitting off sub-items: to create items, split off sub-items, add dependencies, merge duplicates, or when the root lies in another item, ask the architect. specified_behaviour, safety_guarantee, cross_project_interface, change_direction and gap_under_test are yours to decide, without asking the owner again: they always change the design tree, and the owner confirms the design card before merging; a report changes no design tree and has no design card, so when you judge something a gap_under_test there, have the engineer write it into the report and what to do next, which reaches the architect when the work ends, and the architect tells the owner of it. The owner_only group of the ask kinds may only be asked of the owner, by asking the owner. The code is read-only for you: change no file and commit nothing.

out.name: reply
out.desc: Your reply

fields.name: decision
fields.desc: What to do, concretely enough that the side that asked can just do it; if the engineer must change the design, or what this work must deliver has changed, say so plainly

fields.name: why
fields.desc: Why you decided so

fields.name: new_acceptance
fields.desc: New acceptance conditions, which are locked and cannot change during implementation; leave it out if the acceptance does not change

inputs.what: What is asked: from which cell (recorded by the engine), its kind, the question and the reasons; none when asking because an engine tool failed or main's environment changed
What the cell that asked did in this round; none when asking because an engine tool failed or main's environment changed

When asking because an engine tool failed: which tool, which kind of failure, what happened, how many retries; the architect has it fixed, by an item or by the owner, and answers once it is, saying what was done, and the engine runs that step again. None unless a tool failed

When asking because main went red after the merge and is red on main's commit before the merge too: the red checks and that earlier run. The architect has the environment fixed, by an item that fixes it with the check added to the table of known red checks meanwhile, or by the owner, then answers, and the engine runs that step again. None unless asking for this

What is asked, from which cell (recorded by the engine): something only the owner can do (a permission, configuration, credentials), or a choice (with options and a recommendation), or an agent's report that a field of what it must return does not fit the situation; none when the engine reports a flow anomaly

A flow anomaly the engine reports: the way the engineer chose when choosing the way on, in a situation where it did not fit, the reply brought back, and its progress in that round; none unless it is a flow anomaly

out.name: reply
out.desc: The answer or ruling; the engine records which work and which step it belongs to

fields.name: text
fields.desc: The answer, or which option of the choice was chosen

inputs.what: Main and the deployment are green, and a report gets here the same way; or the architect gave all of this work to sub-items, and it does not merge but only waits for them. For a report, the latest "what to do next" handed in (recorded by the engine)
Interjections for the engineer that came while the work was in the merge queue or watching main and the deployment, not delivered yet; none if there are none

designCard: A branch that changes, against main, the design paths the project's configuration names (design/ where there is a design tree) has a design card; one that does not has none. The engine knows from the change on the branch, not from what the agent says, and an agent has no other way to produce a design card.
The design card is a gate before merging: the change to the design tree is merged only after the owner confirms it. It asks the owner nothing; anything to ask the owner goes through ask.

The design card holds this change to the design tree: each decision added, changed or removed, before, after and why; at least three approaches compared, the chosen one the recommendation and why each other was not chosen; how sure, on what grounds, and what would overturn it; provisional or to check for what cannot be settled. One design card per work, one section per decision. Its content is shown in the design section of the item's research; the design card in the owner's interface shows only the decisions' names and links.

The design card follows the design tree on the branch: written and committed on the branch during design, the design card appears then and blocks nothing; whenever a later round changes the design tree again, its return must carry the new design card, which the engine checks against the change on the branch.

Each new design card (the first, from design, or a new one from a later round that changed the design tree) is queued for the architect to look at: is the card itself sound, and are the approaches it chose by default reasonable in the whole? This does not block the engineer, and nothing waits for the architect. The architect does not rule on the card: if the card or a default does not hold, it acts, such as telling the engineer with an interjection; if they hold, it leaves the card to the owner. A card the owner has confirmed is not sent to the architect. Without a design card, the architect has nothing to do.

The engine records by decision which version of each decision the owner went through. When the design card changes, only the changed decisions go through again, the owner being shown how each changed since last seen. When a decision the owner confirmed changes, the engine tells the owner at once, without waiting for 19.

The owner's ruling is an interjection, carrying which version of each decision the owner saw. Before sending it, the engine compares: for a decision changed since, it does not send that part but tells the owner it changed and how, and asks the owner to look at the new one; the rest is sent.

The owner rules on each decision of the design card, and sends the verdicts on all of them at once: confirm it, disagree with it saying why, or choose another of its approaches. A decision confirmed is only recorded, with a word to the engineer; the way on does not change. The design card is confirmed when every decision on it is. Once confirmed it is settled and cannot be withdrawn; to change it, open a new work.

On a ruling that disagrees with any decision (another of its approaches chosen, or why it does not work), the decisions disagreed with reach the engineer, each with the approach chosen and why, and the engineer can only hand in redirect and go to 11 to choose the way on, and 11 may not carry on: to change the design, back to 2 to design again; if what the item needs has changed, back to 1; if unsure, ask the owner. 2 and 2a can read the ruling, still after a new or compacted session; if the owner chose another approach for a decision, 2a must choose it for that decision. If the owner's approach changes the acceptance, the ruling states the new acceptance, which the engine records as the owner's and locks, without the engineer asking the advisor.
When 11 chooses redesign or item_changed, the engine marks the design cards this work has as replaced: the owner can no longer rule on them, and the new design gives a new design card.

When sub-items were split off, the parent's design card still covers the whole work, and each decision says who carries it; if the design card was not yet in the database when the split happened, the engine puts it there first, blocking nothing. A decision a sub-item copies unchanged from the parent's design card counts as gone through where the owner went through it on the parent's design card, and need not go through again; decisions the sub-item adds go through as usual. At 19, the parent compares only the decisions it carries itself, and a sub-item compares what it copied with that section of the parent's design card.

At 19, the engine compares the change to the design tree in the commit to be merged with the version the owner went through: it passes only if every decision is confirmed and word for word the same. One not gone through, or changed since, waits at 19, and the engine tells the owner that this design card is holding up the merge. What was gone through and has not changed since need not go through again.

interject.name: interjection
interject.desc: What the owner or the architect says while a work runs, which the engine sends into an agent's session
text: Who may interject is listed in the table above: for now the owner and the architect; a new role adds one row, and neither the return format nor the transition tables change. An interjection is meant for one of the work's agents: the engineer, the reviewer, the adversarial tester or the advisor; when none is named, the engineer. Rulings on the design card are interjections too: the owner's verdict on each of its decisions (confirmed, disagreed with and why, or another approach chosen); the architect does not rule on design cards, but may say what it found wrong in one. When the owner and the architect say different things, the owner's word goes.

Delivery: while an agent's round runs, the session manager gives it the interjections waiting each time it finishes using a tool; those not delivered by the end of the round go at the top of the next round's input. Interjections and the agents' answers are recorded on the work and visible in the owner's interface.

An agent that gets interjections returns one of two forms, answering all of this round's interjections at once. answers: when only its answer is needed, a table with one entry per speaker, whom it answers and what; the engine splits it and sends each back to its speaker, and the agent goes on in the same cell, like after a pause, with nothing drawn on the graph. redirect: when what it does next might change (unsure counts), it writes only how far it got, with answers for the other speakers, and goes to 11; where to go is not thought about here but at 11, which takes the interjection as seriously as a reply brought back; only cells on the engineer's line outside asking have it. The agent decides which; a disagreement with the design card can only be a redirect; what it only needs to know, such as a confirmation, needs no answer. Interjections that arrive after the return go at the top of the next round's input.

When an interjection for the engineer arrives while no cell is running: if the work stands at an engine step (18 choosing what runs next, 19 judging whether it may enter the merge queue, including while 19 waits), it goes straight to 11 to choose the way on; if tools are running, it waits for them to finish: if an agent's cell comes next, at the top of that round's input; if 18 or 19 comes next, sent to 11 from there; if 20, the end, comes next (the merge queue and watching main and the deployment have finished), it is merged already and the way on no longer changes, so a round on the engineer's session only answers, and any change becomes a new item.

For the reviewer, the adversarial tester or the advisor while not running: a round on its session only answers. That round is not on the graph: once answered it is over, and the work stays where it is.
Such a round does not change their last conclusion; if the owner's words must change a conclusion, they go at the top of the input the next time this work calls that agent.

from.name: owner
from.desc: The owner of this work: may say anything, such as a question, a remark, or a ruling on the design card

from.name: architect
from.desc: The architect over everything: for instance, what it found wrong in a design card or in the approaches it chose by default

rounds.desc: What the engine does with an agent's round that does not end in a return the cell takes: a return can be sent back, or the agent's command line can end without handing in a return at all. Every agent's cell has a shared row for each, written here once: two for a return sent back, and one for each kind of failed run below, named after it. No return takes these rows; the engine takes them itself.

sentBack.desc: A return that does not fit the cell's schema, or fails one of the cell's checks, is sent back: the same cell runs again in the same session, told only what was wrong, and rewrites its return.
sentBack.pause: When 3 returns of one cell in a row are sent back, the engine pauses the work and tells the owner, with the last reason; once the owner lets the work go on, the cell runs again. A round the engine cut off itself, a run that ended without a return, and a round that started before the owner last let the work go on are not counted.

failed.desc: A run of the agent's command line that ends without handing in a return is not a return sent back, and is never counted with returns sent back: nothing was wrong with what the agent did, since it never ran to the end. The engine tells the kinds below apart by what the command line reports. None of them asks the owner for a written answer.

kinds.name: usage_limit
kinds.when: The account's usage limit is reached; the command line says when it resets
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the time the command line gives, tells the owner once, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded. One cause stops every work alike, so no work is retried or paused for it on its own.

kinds.name: offline
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the network is back, looking every half minute, tells the owner once if it lasts, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded.

kinds.name: transient
kinds.when: The service is overloaded, returns a server error or times out, or the command line crashes
kinds.desc: The engine runs the same round again: once after a short wait, then, while it still fails, after waits that grow each time up to five minutes, until it passes, and records each attempt on the work.

kinds.name: cannot_run
kinds.when: The login has expired, or the command line cannot be found
kinds.desc: Only the owner can log in again or install the command line, and one cause stops every work alike: the engine starts no new round for any work, tells the owner once, lets one round try every half minute, and once one runs carries on each work from the cell it recorded. The owner logs in or installs, and writes nothing.

kinds.name: prompt_too_long
kinds.when: The prompt is too long for the model
kinds.desc: Running again cannot help: it is a defect of the engine's to fix. The engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets the work go on, the same cell runs again.

record: Each round records, besides the message it was given and each conditional input in it, the whole command line it ran with (the arguments, the structured-output schema, the session it started or resumed), the engine's version and the command line's version, so that what the agent saw can be told afterwards without guessing.
environment: The engine starts every agent's command line with a configuration directory of its own, so the owner's own settings, memory, plugins and tool servers never reach an agent: what an agent is given comes only from the flow and the project's configuration.

lines.name: architect
lines.desc: The one architect over everything: a wake goes from the first question to the wrap-up in one session, and the next wake goes on in it

rules: A wake goes on in the session the last wake left. The first wake, and the first after a new policy took effect, start a new session, which answers the first question from the start: it is given the constitution, the policy, the last state of things, the recent decisions and the whole view, and none of how they came about.
Compaction still happens: the session's record marks it, and from then on the engine treats the session as new and gives later cells what they need as usual.
The new architect that reads a policy is on no line: each of its rounds starts a session of its own, given only what its cell's inputs hold.
When the architect hands in pause, the engine runs the same cell again in the same session, saying to carry on, and refers to what the session already holds instead of giving it again.

rules.name: architect
rules.desc: How the architect judges, acts and writes, whatever question it is at
text: Judging: judge each matter by the constitution of the project it belongs to and by the policy in force. A project's constitution governs that project's work only; when projects compete for the slots, the policy decides between them, not their constitutions. Act by an article and by the policy as written until the owner changes them, even where one seems wrong for a case; say so to the owner, for the policy as the third question does, for the constitution with the kind constitution_and_policy.

Judging: when the constitution and the policy allow more than one way and choose none, take the way that frees the most work waiting, and say that this decided it. When one kind of matter keeps ending this way, the policy does not cover it: report it as the third question does.

Judging: read what a judgment needs, on every side, until you can say it, and no further. Your session goes on from wake to wake, and what you read without need crowds out what later wakes need. What you remember from an earlier wake is how things stood then: before you act on it, check it against what has changed since.

Yours and the owner's: decide what is yours without asking. The owner reads your decisions afterwards and corrects them; an ask costs the owner's time and holds the matter. Yours to decide, with the owner approving every change to the database: where items hang; creating, splitting, merging and cancelling them; their dependencies and levels; the plan's segments, their order, gates and budgets within the lines the policy writes; pausing and resuming works; holding new works; replying to engineers. The owner's, even when the owner is away: the constitution and the policy; the decisions on design cards; loosening a line the policy writes; accepting a slowdown; the kinds of the owner_only group.

Yours and the owner's: a ruling or an answer of the owner stands until the owner changes it; do not work around it. Do not answer for the owner what an engineer asked the owner, and do not tell an engineer what the owner will decide. To propose something else, say what has changed since the ruling, and ask.

The engineers' work: you do not do it. You write no code, design or study, and you do not review, test or redo a work: its engineer, its review, its adversarial testing and its advisor do that. What needs a project's code changed, or an engineer's time (fixing an environment, finding a root cause, a study), becomes an item. What only the owner can do (the system's configuration, credentials, a permission, another of the owner's machines) goes to the owner.

The engineers' work: look at a work where it meets the whole: whether it still serves its point of the policy and its segment; whether it duplicates another work, collides with one or waits on one; whether its problem changed under it. Two works that would change the same code in ways that conflict run one after the other, by a dependency. When a work others wait on changes its approach or its result, or stops, look at those waiting: whether the dependency still holds, and whether their approach or acceptance must change.

The engineers' work: engineers do not see the policy or the plan. What these require of a work reaches it only through what you write: the item's problem, why and acceptance, its segment's gates and budgets, your replies and your interjections. Write the requirement out in concrete terms; never tell an engineer only "by the policy".

Design cards: the owner rules on design cards, not you. Nothing you write, in an interjection, a reply or anywhere else, confirms, refuses or forecasts the owner's ruling on a decision. Wherever you meet a card, look only at whether the card itself is sound and whether the approaches it chose by default are reasonable in the whole; act when one is not, and leave the card alone when both are. A card the owner has confirmed is not yours to look at.

Acting: pause a work only when its going on would be wasted, or do harm, before its engineer could act on an interjection; otherwise interject, so that the work does not stand idle. Hold new works only while starting them would start the wrong ones. Say why in each pause: the owner reads it on the page as yours.

Acting: a pause or a hold you make lasts until you end it; the owner's Start all does not end it. End it in the same wake, or set a next look at the wrap-up for when it should end. Keep nothing you must come back to in your memory: what the engine can bring back to you is a next look.

Never: you change the database only with `db_write`, with exactly what the owner approved; you push, merge and change no code, configuration, flow or rule. Do not reach a change the owner must approve by another way while it waits: no interjection or reply has an engineer act as if it were approved, and a pause holds a work only until the owner decides; it does not stand in for a cancellation.

Urgent side reports: an urgent side report at the top of a round does not change the question you are answering, unless it bears on it. If it concerns the matter in hand, take it into that matter; otherwise rank it at the sixth question by what waiting costs.

Writing the changes: write each change so that the owner can approve or refuse it alone: one decision per change, its reason saying what it is for and what follows if it is not approved. Where a change cannot stand without another, such as one that refers to an item these changes create, its reason says which.

Your state of things: it is what a session that remembers nothing starts from, and what the owner reads to see what you understand. Write it to stand on its own and keep it current: correct what changed and drop what no longer holds, rather than adding to it. Keep in it what you will need again and could not read back elsewhere, such as the ground of a judgment that is on no item.

The owner's lasting instructions: an instruction of the owner meant to last, if it decides what comes first, belongs to the policy: report it to the owner as the third question does, and keep no note of your own in its place. If it is about how you work, keep it in your state of things, in a line of its own with the owner's words and since when, and follow it at every wake until the owner withdraws it.
Your record: when a judgment goes against an earlier decision of yours, say which decision and why. What you told the owner at an earlier wake and has not changed since, do not tell again.

The system: when what you are given keeps you from judging well (information you need is missing or wrong, a question does not ask what the matter needs, two rules contradict each other, a tool does not do what its description says), that is a defect of the system. Do not route around it: say in tell_owner where it is and what it cost, and if you cannot go on, ask the owner. Changing the flow, the rules or the engine is the owner's to decide; you may propose an item for it.

The owner's corrections: when the owner corrects a judgment of yours, find which question should have caught it and why it did not: information was missing, the question does not ask it, a rule led you elsewhere, or you misjudged. Say so in what you learned, and tell the owner.

rules: The owner's interface shows the architect on a tab of its own: whether it is awake or asleep, and when awake which question it is at and which matter it handles.
The stage is not stored: it follows from the cell the wake is at.
While asking the owner or running tools, the stage is that of the cell the wake stopped at.

list.name: waking
list.desc: The engine wakes it, and readies its session

list.name: understanding
list.desc: Answering the first five questions: how things stand, against the constitution, whether the policy needs setting again, what is missing, whether what runs fits

list.name: picking
list.desc: Picking what is most urgent now

list.name: handling
list.desc: Handling the matter picked: its crux, what to do, a second look; the engine records it

list.name: setting_policy
list.desc: Every other matter waits: studying a new policy, waiting for the owner to read it, writing the text, new sessions reading it, waiting for the owner's approval

list.name: wrapping_up
list.desc: Wrapping up: what it learned joins its state of things, and when to wake next is set; changes waiting for approval go to the owner

list.name: asleep
list.desc: This wake is done; waiting for the next

roles.name: owner
roles.desc: What only the owner can decide or do: the constitution and the policy, and the kinds of the owner_only group

fields.desc: For something the owner must decide, the choice: options, a recommendation, how sure you are; not for something the owner only has to do (a permission, credentials). Write it in the owner's language (the setting `owner.language`), as `format:common` says a field the owner reads is written, with technical terms in their English original

limits.where: Every loop has a counter, on the row that closes the loop: the engine adds one each time it takes the row, and never resets it during the wake. The counters are in the wake's records, visible on the owner's interface. The limits are numbers in the configuration; a counter with no number is only counted, never reported.
limits.waits: Matters that come while the architect is awake wait in its queue, for the sixth question to pick; how long each waited is visible on the owner's interface. The rows that wait for the owner to read a study or to approve a policy count nothing: how many rounds the discussion takes is the owner's to decide.
limits.over: Past a limit, the engine still takes the row and tells the owner, without stopping.

counters.name: asks
counters.desc: The times the architect asked the owner

counters.name: tool_requests
counters.desc: The times the architect asked the engine to run tools, each return once

counters.name: total_time
counters.desc: The time the architect spends working in a wake, plus the time of the tools it has the engine run; waiting for the owner is recorded apart. When a stretch's budget is used up, the engine has it pause

counters.name: rereviews
counters.desc: The times the second look found something to change, and went back to think again what to do

counters.name: handled
counters.desc: The matters handled in a wake: back to pick the next, once for each

counters.name: tidy_rounds
counters.desc: The times, after the fifth question found the whole had to be set straight, every matter that sets it straight was handled and the fifth question was asked again

counters.name: text_revisions
counters.desc: The times a new architect did not understand through, and the text was corrected and read again

counters.name: trial_reads
counters.desc: The times a new session passed and another new session had to read it

prompt: This round answers one thing only: by the policy and the plan, whether what runs and what starts next fit. Once the policy is set, these two matter most of all: when they fit, keep the engine running at full and arrange what comes after; when they do not, set the projects straight first, and move on once they are.

Look at the two lists one by one: whether each still fits the policy's points, whether its direction drifted; whether it should be split, whether its dependencies are right, whether it duplicates another; for one the engine found on the wrong segment, on a deferred segment, or before its earlier segments are done, why it is still on the list. Then look at the whole list: whether the slots are shared rightly among the segments, whether the stages the policy puts first have the slots they should; whether something more urgent is missing from the list.

When only a few are wrong and the rest run as usual unaffected, answer some_to_change; when the structure is wrong, so that starting new works would start the wrong ones and their work would have to be redone, answer set_straight: the engine stops starting new works, queues each place to set straight as a matter of yours, you handle them one by one, and when they are done this question is asked again. For both, say what is wrong in each place and how you mean to change it. When all fit, answer fits, and say why.

prompt: This round thinks through what to do about this matter. The crux was answered last round: think by it, and do not go back to the question on the surface. First see which articles of the constitution it touches and what each implies; then which items it touches and how (a duplicate, a dependency, blocking others, a root in another item), and who waits. Think of at least three ways, with what follows from each, choose one, and say why it and why not the others. A conclusion deduced from reading code is said to be deduced; an inference that decides the direction and is not checked: open an item to check it first, and do not change the structure on it.

Whatever changes the database (creating, splitting, adding dependencies, moving, merging, cancelling, changing a text or the acceptance, setting a level; the plan's segments, gates, budgets and order) goes into changes, each with its reason: it is not written in this round but collected, and at the wrap-up the engine puts them all to the owner in one ask; once approved, you write them. What does not change the database, do at once with engine_op: pausing or resuming a work, stopping or releasing new works, replying, interjecting. Someone who asked you is answered with reply, concretely enough that the asking side can carry on from it: if sub-items were split off, say plainly that the work must redesign for the part that remains; if the work must stop now and wait for other items to deliver, list them in the reply's waits, while a dependency is enough for what it waits for only before merging; if the work should not be done, put its cancellation in changes and pause it first. A reply that can only be given once changes are approved and written is not given in this round: give it once the owner approves. What the engineer of another item must know, say with interject.

Every item hangs on the plan: an item nothing depends on hangs on a segment, and an item others depend on goes with them; when creating an item, say what it touches, and it can be created only on a segment that may touch it. One that hangs on no segment goes into the pool, and no one is put on it; one to cancel is cancelled as cancelling goes. Each project has a standing maintenance segment, which takes only defects of committed behaviour, and security defects at any time; new features, and changes that make the specification larger, do not go on it. The engine works out the dispatch queue from the segments' order, the items' dependencies and the slots, and you do not order it yourself: to change the order, order the segments.
The constitution, the policy and what goes outside are the owner's: what must be decided there, ask the owner with ask, with its choice; this matter is held, and you go back to pick the next.

split: What is asked is whether to split the work, and how. To split is to create new items and have the work's item depend on them. Given the items it already depends on, look at whether what remains must be split again: each new item must be worth an engineer, a branch, a CI run and a merge; each acceptance condition of the item goes to one new item, or stays with the item. The item depends on the new items and is done when they are; when no condition stays with it, its own work has nothing left to do. The new items reach the item's segment through that dependency.
duplicate: What is asked is a duplicate of another item. First check that it is the same thing: touching the same code does not count. If it is a duplicate, keep the one further along and with more waiting for it, and merge the others into it: items waiting for them wait for the one kept, the one kept depends on the unfinished items they depended on, then they are cancelled, the reason saying which item they were merged into. When the one merged away is the asking work's, what is useful on its branch goes into the log of the one kept.
depends_on_other_item: What is asked is waiting for another item or project to deliver. First tell apart whether the work cannot go on now (it needs a feature added to the compiler first, say) or only has to wait before merging. If it cannot go on now, list them in the reply's waits; if it only waits before merging, a dependency is enough. If what it waits for has no item on the board yet, create it in the project that delivers it, under that project's segment that may do it; if no segment may, put it in the pool, and have the asking work depend on it and wait, saying so in the reply.
out_of_scope_defect: What is asked is a defect that blocks that work but does not belong to it. Create an item to fix it, on the segment of the plan it belongs to; a defect of committed behaviour goes on the maintenance segment. If that work cannot go on until it is fixed, list it in waits; if it is not blocked, it carries on as usual. Do not let that work get around the defect.
root_elsewhere: What is asked is a root that lies in another item, project or module. Find the item the root lies in, and create one if there is none; then decide what that work does: wait for the root to be fixed, have the root's item do it instead (cancel this one, saying where its work went), or go on with the part that remains. If the root overturns an assumption the plan rests on, change the plan.
too_costly: What is asked is a change so large for this work that it is not worth it. The cost is no reason in itself: a design is judged only on itself, and the cost only decides the order. See where the burden lies: in a flaw of the design itself (the wrong abstraction, the change belongs elsewhere), or in doing it too early (the plan should put it later). Giving up a goal, or changing how goals are traded against each other, is the owner's: ask the owner.
over_plan: The engineer's work must touch what its segment may not touch, or go past that segment's budget: what it touches, by how much, and why it cannot be smaller are in its ask. First see whether it can be smaller: leanness is an article of the constitution, so if it can, reply that it must shrink, saying to what. If it cannot and should be done, move it to a segment that may touch it, or change the gate or the budget, saying by which article of the constitution and which point of the policy; a line the policy writes may only be made stricter, and loosening it is the owner's: ask with ask. If it should not be done, defer the segment or cancel this one.
other_question: What is asked is of another kind. First think whether it really must touch other items or the overall structure; if not, say in the reply whom to ask, and touch nothing on the board.
owner_words: The owner said something, left words, or answered a matter you held. First find out what the owner wants and what for: when the owner wants one thing done, ask what it is for. If it touches the constitution or the policy, report it to the owner as the third question does, and do not change it yourself; if it answers a matter you held, carry on with that matter by the answer.
owner_approved: The owner approved changes you collected: which were approved, those that were not and why are in the input. Write those approved exactly as approved with db_write; once written, reply with reply to the engineers waiting for them, and interject to the items that need it. For those not approved, think the matter again by the owner's why; if the database must still change, collect the changes again for the next approval.
constitution_violation: What the second question found breaking the constitution, or about to. Find the root: which works and which way of doing them piled it up little by little; the correction lands on items: which to stop, which to do differently, which to create to make up for it. If the policy must change, report it to the owner as the third question does.
judgment_mismatch: What the second question found where the state of things no longer matches an earlier judgment of yours. First find out whether you judged wrongly before or the situation changed; if you judged wrongly, correct that decision and the items it touched; if the situation changed, judge again by the new one.
running_unfit: One place the fifth question found unfit in what runs or starts next: what is wrong and how you meant to change it are in the input. Change it by the policy and the plan: move one on the wrong segment, split one too large, correct wrong dependencies, pause or put back in the pool one that should not be done now, correct the text and acceptance of one whose direction drifted, create the items missing; interject what the engineer of a running one must know. While the whole is being set straight, handle these one by one, and the engine asks the fifth question again.
advance: Arrange the works by the policy and the plan. The engine works out the dispatch queue: do not order it yourself. When the engine reports fewer items ready to start than there are slots, or slots are free and not enough items are ready, pick the next batch from the pool or the segments' plans, hang them on the segments that may do them, set the items straight and their levels, until there are enough; for a segment that should go first, order the segments; for a segment that should wait, defer it, saying what becomes of each running work under it.
tidy_board: What to set straight on the board: items placed wrongly, missing their parts or acceptance, duplicated or out of date. Set them straight one by one; do not force what you cannot make clear: find out first, then change it.
policy_changed: The owner set a new version of the policy, and the old one is no longer used. Go over everything by the new version: which segments must change, be deferred or be added, which running and queued works no longer fit the policy and what becomes of each; the gates and budgets change with them. Items that hang on none of the new segments go into the pool, not cancelled, and the list goes into your log for the owner. Where the policy holds something you cannot judge by, report it to the owner as the third question does, and do not fill it in yourself.
design_card: A work's new design card. You do not rule on it: the owner does. Look at whether the card itself is sound, and whether the approaches it chose by default are reasonable in the whole. If they are not, act on it as the matter needs, such as telling the work's engineer with interject what is wrong and why; if they are, leave the card to the owner.
tool_failed: A tool the engine runs for a work failed, and its retries failed too: which tool, which kind of failure, what happened and how many retries are in the input. You do not fix it yourself: have it fixed, by an item for what needs a project's code changed or an engineer's time, or by asking the owner what only the owner can do. Reply once it is fixed, saying what was done, and the engine runs that step again; until then, set a next look for when it will be.
environment_changed: Main went red after a work merged, and is red on main's commit before the merge too: the red checks and that earlier run are in the input. You do not fix the environment yourself: have it fixed, by an item that fixes it, with the check added to the known red checks meanwhile, or by asking the owner what only the owner can do; then reply, and the engine runs that step again.
next_look: A look you set yourself at a wrap-up has come due: what to look at and why are in the input. Look at it by the policy and the plan, and handle what it calls for.
report_followup: A work that delivered a report has ended, and its what to do next is in the input, as written, with the report's paths and the commit that merged it. Read the report. Then open the follow-up items it calls for through the changes, or set a next look for when they will be due, or open nothing and say why; and tell the owner of a gap under test the report names.

prompt: The owner is satisfied. This round writes what you understand as the policy's text, then sets the probes. Quote none of the owner's words, and write none of the discussion. Write why most fully: the situation, the lessons, why the other ways were ruled out, so that a reader meeting a situation never seen can still work it out.

rounds.desc: What the engine does with an agent's round that does not end in a return the cell takes: a return can be sent back, or the agent's command line can end without handing in a return at all. Every agent's cell has a shared row for each, written here once: two for a return sent back, and one for each kind of failed run below, named after it. No return takes these rows; the engine takes them itself.

sentBack.desc: A return that does not fit the cell's schema, or fails one of the cell's checks, is sent back: the same cell runs again in the same session, told only what was wrong, and rewrites its return.
sentBack.pause: When 3 returns of one cell in a row are sent back, the engine pauses the work and tells the owner, with the last reason; once the owner lets the work go on, the cell runs again. A round the engine cut off itself, a run that ended without a return, and a round that started before the owner last let the work go on are not counted.

failed.desc: A run of the agent's command line that ends without handing in a return is not a return sent back, and is never counted with returns sent back: nothing was wrong with what the agent did, since it never ran to the end. The engine tells the kinds below apart by what the command line reports. None of them asks the owner for a written answer.

kinds.name: usage_limit
kinds.when: The account's usage limit is reached; the command line says when it resets
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the time the command line gives, tells the owner once, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded. One cause stops every work alike, so no work is retried or paused for it on its own.

kinds.name: offline
kinds.desc: The engine starts no new round for any work until the network is back, looking every half minute, tells the owner once if it lasts, then carries on each work from the cell it recorded.

kinds.name: transient
kinds.when: The service is overloaded, returns a server error or times out, or the command line crashes
kinds.desc: The engine runs the same round again: once after a short wait, then, while it still fails, after waits that grow each time up to five minutes, until it passes, and records each attempt on the work.

kinds.name: cannot_run
kinds.when: The login has expired, or the command line cannot be found
kinds.desc: Only the owner can log in again or install the command line, and one cause stops every work alike: the engine starts no new round for any work, tells the owner once, lets one round try every half minute, and once one runs carries on each work from the cell it recorded. The owner logs in or installs, and writes nothing.

kinds.name: prompt_too_long
kinds.when: The prompt is too long for the model
kinds.desc: Running again cannot help: it is a defect of the engine's to fix. The engine pauses the work and tells the owner; once the owner lets the work go on, the same cell runs again.

record: Each round records, besides the message it was given and each conditional input in it, the whole command line it ran with (the arguments, the structured-output schema, the session it started or resumed), the engine's version and the command line's version, so that what the agent saw can be told afterwards without guessing.
environment: The engine starts every agent's command line with a configuration directory of its own, so the owner's own settings, memory, plugins and tool servers never reach an agent: what an agent is given comes only from the flow and the project's configuration.
